clinicalPearls: An autoimmune cause of vitamin B12 deficiency resulting from destruction of gastric parietal cells and loss of intrinsic factor
Produces a macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia, often with a raised mean cell volume, hypersegmented neutrophils and oval macrocytes on the film
Neurological features include subacute combined degeneration of the cord with paraesthesiae, sensory ataxia and impaired proprioception
Intrinsic-factor antibodies are specific but insensitive, whereas parietal-cell antibodies are sensitive but less specific
Autoimmune atrophic gastritis underlies the condition and carries an increased risk of gastric carcinoma and carcinoid tumours
Associated with other autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease, vitiligo and type 1 diabetes
Management is lifelong vitamin B12 replacement, and neurological damage may become irreversible if treatment is delayed
Giving folate alone to a B12-deficient patient can precipitate or worsen neurological deterioration
reference.pathophysiology: Pernicious anaemia is caused by autoimmune destruction of the gastric mucosa. Immune attack on parietal cells produces atrophic gastritis and abolishes secretion of intrinsic factor, the protein required to bind dietary vitamin B12 and enable its absorption in the terminal ileum. Autoantibodies to intrinsic factor further block this process. The resulting B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, causing megaloblastic maturation in the marrow with ineffective erythropoiesis and a macrocytic anaemia. Because B12 is also required for myelin metabolism, deficiency damages the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, producing subacute combined degeneration. Loss of acid and intrinsic factor secretion also impairs absorption of other nutrients and predisposes to gastric neoplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Malabsorption such as coeliac disease or ileal resection
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film showing macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils
Serum vitamin B12, typically low, with folate to assess for combined deficiency
Intrinsic-factor antibodies, highly specific for the diagnosis
Parietal-cell antibodies, sensitive but less specific
Markers of ineffective erythropoiesis such as raised lactate dehydrogenase and bilirubin
Endoscopy and gastric biopsy where atrophic gastritis or neoplasia is suspected
redFlags: Neurological signs of subacute combined degeneration requiring prompt replacement
Alarm symptoms suggesting gastric carcinoma in a patient with atrophic gastritis
Pancytopenia from profound megaloblastic marrow failure
reference.prognosis: Haematological recovery with vitamin B12 replacement is excellent and rapid, but neurological deficits may only partly resolve if treatment is delayed, and lifelong surveillance is needed for the associated risk of gastric malignancy.
pitfalls: Giving folate without B12 and precipitating neurological deterioration
Excluding the diagnosis on a normal mean cell volume, which can occur with coexisting iron deficiency
Overlooking neurological features that may precede overt anaemia
Failing to consider the increased long-term risk of gastric carcinoma
